title: Why Use Cronjob?
description: Schedule SQL queries to run on a [cron expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron) directly from inside DuckDB — no external scheduler, no shell wrapper, no extra process. The catch is the scope: schedules live in memory inside the running DuckDB process. When the process exits, every job is forgotten. Best fit when DuckDB is already a long-running service (a server, a daemon, an analytics worker), not a CLI you start and stop.

sections.title: What this extension is for
sections.description: Cronjob turns a long-running DuckDB process into its own task scheduler. Register a SQL query against a cron expression and DuckDB fires it on schedule — useful when the work is already SQL and you want to keep it that way.

bulletPoints.label: Periodic refresh of materialized data
bulletPoints.description: Rebuild a rollup table every 5 minutes, or recompute a daily aggregate at 02:00 — wrap a [`CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/create_table) in [`cron`](#cron) and the scheduler keeps it current as long as the process is up.

bulletPoints.label: Recurring exports
bulletPoints.description: Schedule a [`COPY ... TO`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/copy) to write Parquet, CSV, or JSON to disk / S3 on a cadence. Pair with the [`httpfs`](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/httpfs/overview) extension for cloud destinations.

bulletPoints.label: Periodic webhook / Slack alerts
bulletPoints.description: Combine with the [`http_client`](/products/extensions/http_client) or [`webmacro`](/products/extensions/webmacro) extensions: a scheduled query fires an HTTP POST whenever a metric crosses a threshold.

bulletPoints.label: Maintenance tasks
bulletPoints.description: Schedule [`ANALYZE`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/analyze), `VACUUM`, statistics rebuilds, log-table pruning, or any other housekeeping that should happen on a cadence rather than on every query.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: [`cron(query, schedule)`](#cron) registers an entry in an in-memory job table managed by the extension. A background thread inside the DuckDB process wakes on the cron tick, executes the registered SQL through the same connection, and records the result in [`cron_jobs`](#cron_jobs).

bulletPoints.label: Six-field cron expressions
bulletPoints.description: Schedules use the six-field form `second minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`, with the standard `*`, `?`, `,`, `-`, `/` operators and `MON`–`SUN` weekday names. Sanity-check expressions on [crontab.guru](https://crontab.guru/) (note: crontab.guru parses the five-field POSIX form — Cronjob's leading `seconds` field is an extension).

bulletPoints.label: In-memory job registry
bulletPoints.description: Jobs live in process memory only. There is no table on disk, no WAL entry, no cluster coordination. [`cron_jobs`](#cron_jobs) is the introspection table; [`cron_delete`](#cron_delete) is the un-register call.

bulletPoints.label: Same connection, same access
bulletPoints.description: Scheduled queries run against the database the scheduler was registered from, with the same access rights. Anything you can run interactively, you can schedule.

bulletPoints.label: No persistence
bulletPoints.description: Restart the process and every registration is gone. There is no file to delete, no stale entry to clean up — and equally, no resume after a crash. Restart-safe scheduling lives outside this extension.

sections.title: Production caveats
sections.description: The fundamentals to internalize before scheduling anything important.

bulletPoints.label: Schedules die with the process
bulletPoints.description: This is the central caveat. A `kill -9`, a deploy, an OOM, or a clean shutdown all wipe the registry — there is no resume. If the work needs to happen on a wall-clock cadence regardless of process state, drive the run from an external orchestrator (system [`cron(8)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/cron.8.html), [`systemd` timers](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.timer.html), [Kubernetes CronJob](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/)) and have *that* invoke DuckDB.

bulletPoints.label: No multi-process coordination
bulletPoints.description: Two DuckDB processes that both load Cronjob and register the same job will both run it. There is no leader election, no lease — pick one process to own the schedule, or de-duplicate downstream.

bulletPoints.label: Errors are recorded, not retried
bulletPoints.description: A failed query writes its error into `last_result` in [`cron_jobs`](#cron_jobs). The extension does not retry, back off, or alert — wrap your scheduled query in its own error-reporting logic (write to an audit table, fire a webhook) if you need notification.

bulletPoints.label: Long-running queries block the next tick
bulletPoints.description: Each registered job is single-threaded against itself. If a query takes longer than the schedule interval, the next tick waits — no overlap, no parallel runs of the same job.

bulletPoints.label: Experimental status
bulletPoints.description: Marked experimental upstream. The function surface is small and stable in spirit, but pin a known-good extension version in production until it's promoted.

useCases.title: Refresh a rollup table on a cadence
useCases.description: [`CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/create_table) wrapped in [`cron`](#cron) — the simplest path to an always-fresh aggregate without an external scheduler.

useCases.title: Periodic exports to disk or S3
useCases.description: Schedule a [`COPY ... TO`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/copy) to write Parquet to a local path or, with [`httpfs`](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/httpfs/overview), to S3 / GCS — daily reports without leaving SQL.

useCases.title: Threshold-triggered webhooks
useCases.description: Pair with the [`http_client`](/products/extensions/http_client) extension: a query that POSTs to a Slack / PagerDuty webhook whenever a metric crosses a threshold, scheduled to run every minute.

useCases.title: Routine maintenance
useCases.description: Schedule [`ANALYZE`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/analyze), prune log tables older than N days, or rebuild secondary indexes — work that doesn't belong on the hot path of any single query.
